newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK - Heat seen struggling despite cold front.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK - Heat seen struggling despite cold front.

text.p: U.S. heating oil prices will have difficulty advancing this week despite the expected arrival of freezing temperatures by mid-week, traders and analysts said, because of continued strong U.S. production and ample supplies in the key East Coast market.

"Barrels are not hard to find," said one New York trader, noting that heating oil differentials Monday morning remained about 0.25 cent a gallon below December futures prices posted on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
"The fact that it's selling at a discount to NYMEX confirms that heating oil is not tight," he added.
Many traders said the market has already factored in a cold front expected to hit the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, by Wednesday.
"The weather is old news. Forecasts may have already boosted the market as far as it can," said Smith Barney energy analyst John Saucer.
Saucer said he was downbeat on heat, at least short term, because of industry data showing a "very high" production rate of almost 3.6 million barrels per day. "It limits the upside."

Forecasters said the Northeast U.S. should see temperatures -- about one degree Fahrenheit above the seasonal norm on Monday -- drop to five or 10 degrees below the normal range by Wednesday as a cold front now hovering over the Midwest drifts toward the Atlantic.

"It's twenty five (degrees F) below zero in North Dakota today and the Northeast should get a shot of that cold air by Wednesday or Thursday," said Weather Services Corp. senior meterologist Mike Palmerino.
Differentials on spot Gulf Coast heating oil, meanwhile, were pegged at about 3.10 cents below December futures on Monday, little changed over the past week.

"Supply is more than adequate," one Gulf trader said, adding all-out production forced the Colonial Pipeline last week to extend space allocation on its Texas-to-New York distillate line through the month of December.
Turning to gasoline, traders said firm demand and tight supplies should offer good support in both the Gulf and New York Harbor.
But one Gulf trader countered with a bearish note, saying some players might begin trimming gasoline purchases to minimize end-of-year "ad valorem" taxes on inventories.

Despite higher output in the Midwest -- refineries in the region reported operating above 98 percent of capacity in the latest API survey -- gasoline basis in Chicago and the Group Three market around Kansas City, Mo., has remained strong.

Refiner buying by Conoco, Coastal and Texaco contributed to the firmness in cash unleaded prices last week, and gasoline supplies remained thin even though refiners were operating at a blistering pace.

The Williams pipeline system, a key barometer of stocks in the Group Three market, reported a relatively thin 18-day supply of gasoline stocks and a relatively large 32-day supply of low sulphur diesel on hand.
Most Chicago traders wound down trade in late-November deliveries last week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday this Thursday, and were shifting focus to early December barrels.
-- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632
